codebook.source: MONK-2 problem (Thrun et al. 1991), PMLB 'monk2' deduplicated to the 432 input configurations; attributes a1-a6 are abstract (no real-world meaning), so statements are phrased in rule terms on the attribute values

ann_22.text: This part of the model acts on 112 of the 345 training cases, none of which is actually 'yes'.
For the typical case it acts on, which has every attribute at its first value, it clearly moves the predicted probability of 'yes' from above 99% without the part to below 1% with it.
For the typical case overall, moving a1, a3 or a6 away from its first value through this part clearly raises the predicted probability of 'yes' from below 1% to about 99%.
For the typical case it acts on, giving a2 or a4 its first value slightly lowers it, staying below 1%.
Through this part the effects of a3, a4 and a6 also depend slightly on one another and on a2, with the typical case staying at about 3% or below.

ann_23.text: This part of the model reads a2 and a5 and acts on 259 of the 345 training cases, 82 of which are actually 'yes'.
For the typical case it acts on (a1 = 1, a2 = 1, a3 = 1, a4 = 2, a5 = 1, a6 = 1), it slightly changes the predicted probability of 'yes', which stays below 1% (on the training data only).

Through this part, giving a2 its first value or giving a5 the value 4 slightly lowers the predicted probability of 'yes', and the a2 effect is slightly larger when a5 is something other than 4 (on the training data only).

ann_24.text: Through this part, moving a3 or a6 away from its first value slightly lowers the predicted probability of 'yes' for the typical case, which stays below 1%.
Moving a1 away from its first value, or a4 from 2 to 3, also slightly lowers it, and giving a2 or a4 its first value slightly raises it (on the training data only).
Moving a5 away from its first value, in contrast, slightly raises it (on the training data only).

ann_25.text: In the model as a whole, moving a5 away from its first value slightly raises the predicted probability of 'yes' for the typical case, which stays below 1% (on the training data only).
Changing a4 from 2 to 3 slightly lowers it, so the model does not treat the two other values of a4 alike.

ann_22.original: An at-least-three-of-five indicator detector over {a1=1, a2=1, a3=1, a4=1, a6=1} that ignores a5. Node 419 = ReLU(-4.585 + 4.540 z(a1:1) + 5.631 z(a2:1) - 7.622 z(a3:2) + 5.529 z(a4:1) + 6.541 z(a6:1) - 1.371 z(a6:2)). In indicator terms the pre-activation is -31.60 (no indicators active) plus a1 +9.50, a2 +11.92, a3 +15.25 (via the complement a3:2), a4 +11.95, a6 +15.83 (via a6:1 and the complement a6:2). The largest two-indicator sum (a3+a6 = 31.08) leaves it at -0.52 (off); the smallest three-indicator sum (a1+a2+a4 = 33.37) reaches +1.76 (on). So the unit fires iff at least three of these five indicators are active. Evidence (train, n=345, and all 432 configurations): fires iff >=3 of the five indicators hold, agreement 1.0; max pre-activation with <=2 active is -0.525. Sensitivity is spread over all six entries, smallest for a6:2 (0.44).
ann_22.proposed: This part acts on 112 training cases, none of them actually 'yes', and pushes their predicted probability of 'yes' below 1%; through it, moving a1, a3 or a6 away from its first value takes the typical case from below 1% to about 99%.

ann_23.original: A small serial chain giving a bonus when neither a2=1 nor a5=4. Node 1701 = ReLU(0.632 + 0.732 z(a2:1)) is always positive (0.111 if a2!=1, 1.660 if a2=1), so it is a linear relay of a2:1. Node 2480 = ReLU(0.900 - 1.120 z(a5:4) - 0.915 * n1701) takes three values: 1.445 when a2!=1 and a5!=4, 0.026 when a2=1 and a5!=4, and 0 when a5=4 (ReLU clips). Through its +0.618 readout it adds about +0.89 to the output logit only when a2!=1 and a5!=4: a weak, AND-of-negations nudge. Evidence (train, n=345): n2480 > 1 iff a2!=1 and a5!=4, agreement 1.0. Local ablation: zeroing its readout flips only 2 train predictions and slightly raises train accuracy (0.901 -> 0.907), so it is near-vestigial.
ann_23.proposed: A small part that slightly lowers the predicted probability of 'yes' when a2 = 1 or a5 = 4 (on the training data only).

ann_24.original: A linear indicator ramp with an a5=1 veto. Evaluated per attribute value, the direct connections contribute: a1 = 1/2/3: +3.85/-2.84/-1.31; a2 = 1/other: +7.00/-3.54; a3 = 1/2: +3.93/-4.14; a4 = 1/2/3: +2.98/-0.63/-2.19; a6 = 1/2: +4.40/-4.63. So for a1,a2,a3,a4,a6 the first value raises the sum by 3.6 to 10.5 units, making the sum rise roughly linearly with the number of these indicators. Attribute a5 is inverted: a5 = 1/2/3/4 contributes -6.25/+2.51/+1.90/+1.90, i.e. a5=1 is an 8-unit penalty rather than a positive indicator. Together with the output bias (+1.855) the ramp crosses zero between one and two active indicators among {a1,a2,a3,a4,a6} when a5!=1, and an a5=1 pushes it back below zero. Evidence: the per-value contributions are exact (linear in the one-hot columns); sensitivity on train is largest for a2:1 (4.98), a3:1 (4.04), a6:2 (3.73), a5:1 (3.54), a1:2 (3.16). Note a5=1 acts as a veto, not an indicator.
ann_24.proposed: This part slightly lowers the predicted probability of 'yes' when a1, a3 or a6 moves away from its first value and slightly raises it when a2 or a4 takes its first value, but it treats a5 the other way round: a5 away from its first value slightly raises it.

ann_25.original: The output composes the three children additively under the sigmoid: logit = 1.855 + Ramp - 7.413*Gate + 0.618*Chain. Ramp: the first value of a1,a2,a3,a4,a6 raises the sum (by 3.6-10.5 each), so with the bias it crosses zero between one and two active indicators among {a1=1,a2=1,a3=1,a4=1,a6=1} when a5!=1 (lower edge of a response peak); a5=1 instead costs about 8 logit units, pushing count-two cases below zero (an a5=1 veto). Gate: when three or more of the same five indicators are active it fires (pre-activation >=1.76) and its -7.41 readout overwhelms the Ramp (upper edge). Chain: +0.89 when a2!=1 and a5!=4; flips only 2 train predictions and is near-vestigial. Net: the model predicts positive approximately iff exactly two of {a1=1,a2=1,a3=1,a4=1,a6=1} hold AND a5!=1. Evidence (train, n=345): this rule agrees with the model on 331/345 rows (418/432 of all configurations); the 14 disagreements are near-boundary cases (|logit| < 1.8). Train accuracy 0.901, AUC 0.915; every train positive with a5=1 and exactly one other indicator (20 rows) is missed. Ablation: zeroing the gate drops train accuracy to 0.58; zeroing the chain gives 0.907. Inputs a2:2, a2:3, a4:2, a5:3 have no enabled edges and are zero-effect entries (sensitivity exactly 0).
ann_25.proposed: In the model as a whole, a5 away from its first value slightly raises the predicted probability of 'yes' (on the training data only) and a4 = 3 slightly lowers it compared with a4 = 2.

summary.text: One part of the model acts on 112 of the 345 training cases, none of which is actually 'yes'.
For the typical case this part acts on, which has every attribute at its first value, it clearly moves the predicted probability of 'yes' from above 99% without the part to below 1% with it.

For the typical case overall (the most common value of each attribute: a1 = 1, a2 = 3, a3 = 1, a4 = 2, a5 = 1, a6 = 1), moving a1, a3 or a6 away from its first value through this part clearly raises the predicted probability of 'yes' from below 1% to about 99%.
In the model as a whole, moving a5 away from its first value slightly raises the predicted probability of 'yes' for the typical case, which stays below 1% (on the training data only).
Changing a4 from 2 to 3 slightly lowers it.

parts.name: count_gate_atleast3_of5
parts.original_hypothesis: An at-least-three-of-five indicator detector over {a1=1, a2=1, a3=1, a4=1, a6=1} that ignores a5. Node 419 = ReLU(-4.585 + 4.540 z(a1:1) + 5.631 z(a2:1) - 7.622 z(a3:2) + 5.529 z(a4:1) + 6.541 z(a6:1) - 1.371 z(a6:2)). In indicator terms the pre-activation is -31.60 (no indicators active) plus a1 +9.50, a2 +11.92, a3 +15.25 (via the complement a3:2), a4 +11.95, a6 +15.83 (via a6:1 and the complement a6:2). The largest two-indicator sum (a3+a6 = 31.08) leaves it at -0.52 (off); the smallest three-indicator sum (a1+a2+a4 = 33.37) reaches +1.76 (on). So the unit fires iff at least three of these five indicators are active. Evidence (train, n=345, and all 432 configurations): fires iff >=3 of the five indicators hold, agreement 1.0; max pre-activation with <=2 active is -0.525. Sensitivity is spread over all six entries, smallest for a6:2 (0.44).

parts.name: linear_indicator_ramp
parts.original_hypothesis: A linear indicator ramp with an a5=1 veto. Evaluated per attribute value, the direct connections contribute: a1 = 1/2/3: +3.85/-2.84/-1.31; a2 = 1/other: +7.00/-3.54; a3 = 1/2: +3.93/-4.14; a4 = 1/2/3: +2.98/-0.63/-2.19; a6 = 1/2: +4.40/-4.63. So for a1,a2,a3,a4,a6 the first value raises the sum by 3.6 to 10.5 units, making the sum rise roughly linearly with the number of these indicators. Attribute a5 is inverted: a5 = 1/2/3/4 contributes -6.25/+2.51/+1.90/+1.90, i.e. a5=1 is an 8-unit penalty rather than a positive indicator. Together with the output bias (+1.855) the ramp crosses zero between one and two active indicators among {a1,a2,a3,a4,a6} when a5!=1, and an a5=1 pushes it back below zero. Evidence: the per-value contributions are exact (linear in the one-hot columns); sensitivity on train is largest for a2:1 (4.98), a3:1 (4.04), a6:2 (3.73), a5:1 (3.54), a1:2 (3.16). Note a5=1 acts as a veto, not an indicator.

parts.name: a2_a5_bonus_chain
parts.original_hypothesis: A small serial chain giving a bonus when neither a2=1 nor a5=4. Node 1701 = ReLU(0.632 + 0.732 z(a2:1)) is always positive (0.111 if a2!=1, 1.660 if a2=1), so it is a linear relay of a2:1. Node 2480 = ReLU(0.900 - 1.120 z(a5:4) - 0.915 * n1701) takes three values: 1.445 when a2!=1 and a5!=4, 0.026 when a2=1 and a5!=4, and 0 when a5=4 (ReLU clips). Through its +0.618 readout it adds about +0.89 to the output logit only when a2!=1 and a5!=4: a weak, AND-of-negations nudge. Evidence (train, n=345): n2480 > 1 iff a2!=1 and a5!=4, agreement 1.0. Local ablation: zeroing its readout flips only 2 train predictions and slightly raises train accuracy (0.901 -> 0.907), so it is near-vestigial.

reference_patient.definition: the typical patient: the median training patient for every number and the most common training category for every category (not a real patient)

confidence_rules.clearly: a meaningful change in predicted risk for a typical patient (at least 5% points), the test split agrees (same sign, and its bootstrap interval over test patients excludes no benefit), and every group has at least 20 training patients
confidence_rules.consistently across patients: the claim holds for at least 90% of training patients (range across patients); this is not a significance statement
confidence_rules.on the training data only: the test split disagrees (opposite sign, or no benefit on test patients) or is unclear (its interval includes no benefit), or no test check is available
confidence_rules.slightly: the change in predicted risk for a typical patient is below 5% points
confidence_rules.the model has little data on this: a compared group has fewer than 20 training patients

settings.effect_scale: log-odds (output pre-activation) for verification; predicted risk for the typical patient for wording
